A submarine is a watercraft — a vehicle built to travel — that can operate fully underwater, beneath the surface of the sea. Unlike a regular ship or boat, which floats on top of water, a submarine can dive down into the water and move through it, hidden from view. It can also rise back up to the surface whenever needed.

Think of it this way: a boat lives on water. A submarine lives in water.

A submarine has a long, cylindrical (tube-like) shape, somewhat like a thick cigar or a large pill. This smooth, rounded shape helps it cut through water efficiently. It has no open deck like a regular ship. Instead, its entire body is sealed shut so that water cannot get inside.

On top of the submarine's body, there is usually a tall, narrow tower called a conning tower or sail. This is where the periscope — a long tube with mirrors that allows people inside to see above the water's surface — is located.

At the back, a submarine has propellers (or a modern pump-jet system) to push it forward, and fins (called planes or hydroplanes) to help it steer and control whether it moves up or down.
How Does It Go Underwater? The Key Mechanism

This is the most important thing to understand about how a submarine works.

A submarine has special hollow chambers built into its body called ballast tanks. These tanks are the secret to diving and surfacing.

  • To dive (go underwater): The submarine opens valves to let seawater flood into the ballast tanks. The added weight of the water makes the submarine heavier than the surrounding water, so it sinks downward.
  • To surface (come back up): The submarine pumps compressed air (pressurized air stored in cylinders) into the ballast tanks, pushing the seawater back out. With less water and more air inside, the submarine becomes lighter than the surrounding water, so it rises upward.

This principle is called buoyancy — the idea that an object sinks when it is heavier than the water it displaces, and floats when it is lighter. A submarine actively controls its own buoyancy to go up or down at will.

The crew controls the depth precisely using the hydroplanes (the fins), angling them like the wings of an airplane tilting up or down.
What Happens to the People Inside?

The crew lives and works inside the sealed, pressurized hull (the main body of the submarine). The air inside is carefully maintained so people can breathe normally, even when the submarine is hundreds of meters underwater.

Modern submarines can stay submerged for weeks or even months at a time. They carry food, fresh water, and equipment for extended journeys. Some submarines generate their own oxygen by splitting water molecules using electricity, in a process called electrolysis.

The environment inside is cramped — space is very limited. Crew members live very close together, sleeping in narrow bunks, sometimes in shifts.

Submarines come in several broad types depending on their purpose:

1. Military Submarines
These are by far the most common type and the reason submarines were originally invented. Military submarines are used by navies (the naval forces of countries) around the world.

  • Attack submarines (SSN): These hunt and destroy enemy ships and other submarines. They are fast and highly maneuverable. They are powered by nuclear reactors or diesel-electric engines.
  • Ballistic missile submarines (SSBN): These are very large submarines that carry nuclear missiles. Their entire purpose is to stay hidden deep underwater as a deterrent — meaning that even if a country is attacked, it can still launch a nuclear counterattack from these hidden submarines. They are almost never used directly in combat; their power comes from the threat of their existence.
  • Diesel-electric submarines: These are conventional (non-nuclear) submarines powered by diesel engines when on or near the surface, and by electric batteries when submerged. They are quieter than nuclear submarines but need to come to periscope depth periodically to recharge their batteries using a device called a snorkel (a breathing tube that reaches above the water).
  • Nuclear-powered submarines: These use a nuclear reactor as their power source. They can stay submerged almost indefinitely (limited only by food supplies and crew endurance), travel at greater speeds, and are used by major naval powers like the USA, Russia, UK, France, China, and India.

2. Research and Scientific Submarines
Scientists use small submarines to explore the deep ocean — to study marine life, underwater geological formations, shipwrecks, volcanic vents, and ocean ecosystems. These are sometimes called submersibles, though the terms overlap.

Famous examples include the vessels that explored the wreck of the Titanic and the craft that have reached the deepest point on Earth, the Mariana Trench.

3. Tourist Submarines
Some tourist destinations operate small submarines that take paying passengers on underwater tours to see coral reefs and marine life. These operate in shallow coastal waters and are purely for sightseeing.

When you read or hear about submarines, you'll often encounter these terms. Knowing them will help you fully understand the word "submarine" in context:

  • Periscope: A tube with mirrors and lenses that lets the crew see above the water's surface while the submarine is just below it.
  • Torpedo: An underwater self-propelled weapon (like a bomb that swims) fired from a submarine to attack enemy ships.
  • Sonar: The technology submarines use to "see" underwater. It works by sending out sound waves and listening for echoes — similar to how bats navigate. Active sonar sends out a ping and listens for the echo; passive sonar only listens for sounds from other vessels.
  • Hull: The main sealed body of the submarine.
  • Depth charge: A weapon dropped into water by enemy ships or aircraft to explode near and damage a submarine.
  • Snorkel: A tube that extends near the surface, allowing a submarine's diesel engines to breathe air (and recharge batteries) without fully surfacing.
  • Surfacing: When a submarine rises completely above the water's surface.
  • Submerging / Diving: When a submarine descends below the water's surface.
  • Crush depth / Collapse depth: The depth at which the water pressure becomes so extreme that the submarine's hull would be crushed. Submarines are engineered to operate well above this limit.
Informal and Extended Uses of the Word

Outside its literal meaning, "submarine" is also used informally in everyday language:

  • Submarine sandwich (sub): A long sandwich made in a long roll of bread, named because its elongated shape resembles a submarine. In everyday conversation, people often just say "sub."
  • Submarine cable: An underwater cable laid along the ocean floor to carry internet data, telephone signals, or electricity between countries and continents. Most of the world's international internet traffic travels through submarine cables.
The Big Picture — Why Submarines Matter

Submarines changed the nature of naval warfare and global power permanently. Their ability to stay hidden makes them one of the most strategically important weapons ever created. During World War I and World War II, German submarines (called U-boats, short for Unterseeboot, meaning "undersea boat") nearly crippled Britain by sinking enormous numbers of supply ships. Today, nuclear-armed submarines are considered the most survivable part of a country's nuclear arsenal — because they are hidden, they are very difficult to destroy in a first strike, making them a powerful deterrent to war.

Beyond warfare, submarines have expanded human knowledge of the deep ocean, which remains one of the least explored environments on Earth.

In one sentence: A submarine is a sealed, self-contained vessel capable of travelling both on and beneath the surface of the ocean, used primarily for military purposes but also for scientific research and exploration.
